rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or fusion strategy is most effective. The most critical uncertainty is establishing a performance baseline against which all other design choices (multiprofile, learned encoders, image modality, multimodal fusion) can be meaningfully compared. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) establishes the simplest and most standard RNA-only baseline. PCA with 2000 components is a neutral, fast, non-learned representation; singleprofile avoids aggregation confounds. This gives a clean performance anchor. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: With a limited budget, the first experiment should be fast to run (PCA is computationally cheap, no image encoder, no aggregation, no fusion) so we get a reliable signal quickly. It directly enables the next logical comparisons: (a) multiprofile RNA with aggregation (configs 002/003) to isolate the effect of aggregation, (b) learned RNA encoders (configs 004-009) to isolate the effect of representation, (c) image-only baselines (configs 010-015) to compare modalities, and (d) multimodal fusion (configs 016+) to test whether integration adds value over the best unimodal result. Starting here avoids confounding multiple design changes in the first data point and gives the strongest interpretive foundation for all subsequent experiments.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), evidence is extremely sparse. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries any predictive signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean, single-variable comparison with config_001 that isolates the modality effect while keeping profile setting (singleprofile) and model simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion) constant. This is the highest-information next step: if image-only performs comparably or better than RNA-only, it validates pursuing multimodal fusion (configs 016–051); if it performs poorly, it redirects budget toward improving the RNA side (encoder, multiprofile). Without this baseline, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable because we could not attribute performance to fusion quality versus the strength of the individual modalities. It is the best use of one experiment to reduce uncertainty about the most consequential design axis.

Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001) achieves 48.5% accuracy while image-only with ResNet50 (config_010) achieves only 20.8%, strongly indicating RNA is the dominant informative modality. This makes the choice of RNA representation the highest-leverage design decision. Uncertainty: We have only tested a linear PCA encoder (n2000). It is unknown whether a learned, nonlinear encoder (scvi_n200) captures biologically meaningful structure that PCA misses, which could substantially shift the performance ceiling. Question tested: config_004 is a clean single-variable comparison against config_001 (same rna_only model, same singleprofile setting; only the encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200), directly isolating the effect of representation quality. Why best next step: Under a tight budget, establishing whether a purpose-built single-cell encoder outperforms PCA determines whether to invest further in encoder choice or instead focus on profile/aggregation/fusion dimensions. If scvi improves accuracy meaningfully, it reshapes the multimodal strategy; if not, PCA suffices and we can redirect budget toward multiprofile or fusion experiments.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_004 (rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) at 0.520 acc, and image-only (resnet50) is very weak at 0.208, confirming RNA is the dominant signal. However, we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile (with aggregation) improves over singleprofile—this is the largest untested design axis, affecting half the configuration space. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation improve performance when using the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200)? config_005 is a clean, single-variable comparison against config_004 (same encoder, same modality; only profile setting and aggregation change). Why this is best: It isolates the multiprofile effect with the simplest aggregation, reducing uncertainty about a high-impact design choice before committing budget to more complex multiprofile variants (transformer, scgpt, or multimodal multiprofile). If multiprofile+avgpool shows no gain, we can deprioritize most multiprofile configs; if it shows gain, we can then test transformer aggregation and multimodal extensions with confidence.

Evidence: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc / 0.628 F1, a large jump over config_004 (same encoder, singleprofile: 0.520). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is a major design lever. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) further improves performance, or whether avgpool is already near-optimal for this encoder. Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding rna_only, multiprofile, and scvi_n200 fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_005. Why best next step: it directly exploits the strongest evidence (best-performing config) to isolate the effect of aggregation, a design choice that will propagate to every future multimodal experiment. If transformer substantially outperforms avgpool, we gain a better aggregation for all downstream fusion experiments; if it does not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget toward encoder or modality questions. This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 yields a large jump (~13 pts) over singleprofile (0.520→0.650), while aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) makes almost no difference (0.650 vs 0.653). Image-only is very weak (0.208). Key uncertainty: Is the multiprofile benefit specific to scvi_n200's learned latent representation, or is it a general property of aggregating multiple profiles regardless of encoder? This experiment (pca_n2000 + multiprofile + avgpool) directly tests that interaction by changing only the profile setting relative to config_001 (pca_n2000 singleprofile, 0.485). If pca_n2000 also jumps substantially, multiprofile is a universal design win and we can focus budget on encoder choice and fusion. If it does not, the benefit is tied to scvi's representation, guiding us toward learned encoders. This is a clean single-variable comparison, more informative than jumping to multimodal (where the weak image modality muddies interpretation) or testing scgpt (which introduces two untested variables at once), making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA multiprofile with scvi_n200 + avgpool (config_005, acc=0.650) and pca_n2000 + avgpool (config_002, acc=0.591) show that the RNA encoder choice contributes ~6 points of accuracy in the multiprofile setting. Aggregation method (avgpool vs transformer) has negligible effect (0.650 vs 0.653). scgpt is the only untested RNA encoder. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 as an RNA encoder in the best-performing multiprofile setting? config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating encoder quality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in multimodal or image-encoder experiments, we need to know the ceiling of the RNA-only pipeline. If scgpt substantially beats scvi_n200, it changes which RNA encoder to pair with image in multimodal configs; if it underperforms, we can confidently anchor multimodal experiments on scvi_n200. This reduces uncertainty about the most impactful design axis (representation) with minimal confounds.

Evidence: RNA-only multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the clear winner (acc 0.653), and we've mapped the RNA encoder ranking (scvi > pca > scgpt) and confirmed aggregation barely matters. However, the image modality is essentially unexplored—config_010 (resnet50, singleprofile) scored only 0.208, near chance. The critical uncertainty is whether a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) can extract any useful signal from the images, or whether the image modality is simply uninformative for this task. Question: config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010 (only the image encoder changes from resnet50 to ViT-L), isolating the effect of representation quality on image signal. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing limited budget in multimodal fusion experiments (configs 016-051), we need to know whether image carries any discriminative information at all. If ViT-L image remains near chance, we can rule out the image modality entirely and focus remaining budget on RNA refinements. If it shows meaningful signal, multimodal fusion becomes a high-value direction. This experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design decision (include image or not) with a minimal, interpretable comparison.

Evidence: Multi-profile RNA with scvi_n200 is the strongest setup (config_005: 0.650 acc, config_006: 0.653 acc), and aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) has negligible impact (~0.3% difference). Image-only models are very weak (~0.21-0.23 acc), raising the question of whether image adds any value when fused with the strong RNA signal. Question: Does adding the image modality (resnet50) to the best RNA multi-profile configuration (scvi_n200, avgpool) improve validation accuracy over the RNA-only baseline of ~0.650, or does it dilute the signal? This is the minimal multimodal extension of config_005—only adding image_encoder and fusion (concat, the simplest option)—so it cleanly isolates the contribution of the image modality. Why this is the best next experiment: Before investing budget in optimizing fusion type, image encoder, or aggregation within the multimodal space, we need to know whether image contributes at all. If config_030 matches or beats 0.650, we have a strong direction to exploit; if it underperforms, we save budget by ruling out the image modality and focusing on RNA-only refinements. Starting with the simpler resnet50 and concat fusion keeps the experiment interpretable.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200/multiprofile achieves 0.650–0.653, while the sole multimodal experiment (config_030: scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) underperforms at 0.632. Image-only models are very weak (0.208–0.227), suggesting the image modality may be adding noise. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the multimodal deficit is due to the relatively weak resnet50 image encoder or a fundamental lack of image signal for this task. Question tested: config_036 swaps only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (the stronger encoder, which was also better in image-only: 0.227 vs 0.208) while holding all other settings identical to config_030. This isolates the effect of image representation quality. Why best next experiment: If even the best available image encoder cannot lift the multimodal model above the RNA-only baseline, we can confidently conclude the image modality is uninformative for this task and redirect remaining budget to RNA-only optimization. If it does help, it reveals that image encoder quality is the bottleneck and justifies further multimodal exploration. This single-variable comparison maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.
